paragraphs.heading: A seesaw of ocean temperature
paragraphs.text: The Indian Ocean Dipole, or IOD, is an irregular oscillation of sea surface temperatures. The western Indian Ocean becomes by turns warmer and then colder than the eastern part. The warmer-west state is called the positive phase and the colder-west state the negative phase, and there is a neutral phase as well. Indian climate researchers from the Indian Institute of Science first identified the IOD in 1999.

paragraphs.heading: What each phase brings
paragraphs.text: In a positive phase, sea surface temperatures in the western Indian Ocean region are higher than average and more rain falls there. The waters of the eastern Indian Ocean cool at the same time, which tends to cause droughts in nearby land areas of Indonesia and Australia. The negative phase brings the opposite conditions: warmer water and more rain in the east, cooler and drier conditions in the west. The strength of the monsoons over the Indian subcontinent is affected by the IOD too.

paragraphs.heading: How often it happens
paragraphs.text: On average, four positive and four negative events occur in each 30-year period, and each event lasts around six months. The record does not always follow that average. Between 1980 and 2009 there were 12 positive IODs, and from 1980 to 1992 there was not a single negative event. Consecutive positive events are extremely rare, with only two cases recorded: 1913–1914, and three in a row from 2006 to 2008. Modelling suggests that consecutive positive events could be expected twice in a 1,000-year period.

paragraphs.heading: Drought in southern Australia
paragraphs.text: A 2009 study at the University of New South Wales showed that drought in Australia's southern half, and the south-east in particular, is significantly correlated with the IOD. In the negative phase, cool water in the western Indian Ocean and warm water off northwest Australia generate winds that pick up moisture from the ocean and sweep down toward southern Australia, delivering higher rainfall. In the positive phase the pattern of ocean temperatures is reversed. The winds weaken and less moisture is picked up and carried across Australia. As a consequence, the south-east gets rainfall well below average while a positive IOD lasts.

paragraphs.heading: Floods in East Africa
paragraphs.text: The East African Short Rains fall between October and December, and a positive IOD is linked to more rain than average in that season. Higher rainfall in the short rains is associated with warm sea surface temperatures in the western Indian Ocean and with low-level westerly winds across the equatorial part of the ocean, which bring moisture over East Africa. The increased rainfall has been found to result in more flooding. At the end of 2019, when a particularly strong positive IOD was under way, East Africa's average rainfall was 300% higher than normal.

paragraphs.heading: Ties to the Pacific and to warming
paragraphs.text: The IOD is one part of the general cycle of global climate, and it interacts with similar phenomena such as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation in the Pacific Ocean. A strong negative IOD that developed in October 2010, coupled with a strong La Niña at the same time, caused the Queensland floods of 2010–2011 and the Victorian floods of 2011. In 2008, Nerilie Abram built an index reaching back to 1846 from coral records taken in the eastern and western Indian Ocean, and it suggested that positive IOD events grew in strength and frequency during the 20th century. The western Indian Ocean is expected to warm at accelerated rates because of climate change, and so to bring positive IODs more often. That is likely to make rainfall more intense during the short rain period over East Africa.
